items.title: John Abercrombie interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001
items.q: which is why I like to play with Nussbaum a lot

ctx.x: Well I’ve always said I mean it’s probably because of my connection to Jim Hall and what he did with Sonny Rollins, I’ve gotten a chance to play with Jim, although I’d like to play with him a little more I mean maybe just one on one, that would be great. We’ve done some on concerts but it’s never been real just sitting down in a room and playing you know. That would be very cool, I’d like to do that. But I’d love to play with Sonny

Rollins. And one drummer that, I’ve played with a lot of the great drummers, DeJohnette, I’ve played with Roy Haynes a few times and I’ve played with you know Billy Hart and just Peter Erskine, Adam Nussbaum, just a whole slew of great drummers, but I haven’t played with Elvin Jones. And I just think that’s got to be great. I mean how can that not be great? I mean it’s impossible, that would be impossible not to feel great playing with him, I mean that’s just — he’s sort of like the epitome somehow of a certain…
[off camera comment] Anything you’d like me to — well — we’ll leave that a mystery.

items.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

ctx.x: You have a pretty good percentage of original material in the trio. Is it a challenge to get your own pieces played these days, other than doing it yourself?

Well the couple of organ records that I’ve done lately I think have been almost all my tunes but maybe a couple of standards. With this band we played some of Adam’s tunes, we played a lot of my tunes which has been really nice, that from the beginning of that, I think the first record was very equal or whatever in the amount of writing. I mean John
basically has always looked for material that we would sound good playing. It doesn’t matter who wrote it. If this works, fine.
